description: Somos uma equipe multidisciplinar, contamos com habilidades nas áreas da Computação, Pedagogia, Análise de Dados, Música, Design e muito trabalho em equipe!!
summary: “The Hidden Sound of the Earth” was developed as a sonification tool that translates images into melodies, allowing anyone to appreciate the beauty of the Earth and the universe. We take different images of the Earth and transform them into melodies, each with its own unique character. “The Hidden Sound of the Earth” is an important step on the long road toward inclusion, enabling more people to fall in love with the world of Astronomy
details:
Algorithmic Pipeline: How Earth Jukebox Translates Pixels into Music

  1. Downscaling & Perceptual Luminance (192px Canvas)
    • The satellite visualization is rendered onto an off-screen canvas at a normalized resolution of 192 horizontal pixels.
    • Pixels are converted into grayscale luminance using human perceptual weights (favoring green wavelengths, where the human eye has the highest photopic sensitivity).
  2. Column Quantization & Vertical Slicing (48 Columns × 15 Bands)
    • The canvas is divided into 48 temporal columns (each representing an active musical beat/note).
    • Vertically, each column is segmented into 15 discrete horizontal bands, computing the mean brightness and average RGB color for each cell.
  3. Pitch Mapping & Smoothing (Top = Treble, Bottom = Bass)
    • Pitch is determined by the brightest band within the column, applying a neighbor-smoothing filter to prevent jitter.
    • Melodic Coherence: Consecutive pitch jumps are constrained to a maximum of 5 scale steps, avoiding erratic leaps and preserving melodic flow.
  4. Harmonic Scale Quantization (Consonance Engine)
    • Raw vertical steps are mathematically mapped to defined musical scales chosen per theme (e.g., Pentatonic, Natural Minor, Lydian). This ensures that every generated frequency snaps into consonance—nothing sounds out of tune.
  5. Dynamic Velocity (Volume from Contrast)
    • The relative brightness of the chosen band—normalized against the minimum and maximum luminance of the entire image—sets the velocity (gain/volume) of the note.
  6. Color-Driven Timbre & Filter Synthesis
    • Green Dominance: Triggers short, percussive envelopes (marimba-like plucks).
    • Warm Tones (Red > Blue): Triggers bright, harmonically rich waveforms (sawtooth).
    • Cool Tones: Triggers soft, sustained pads with gentle attacks.
    • Spectral Filter (Cutoff): Dominant hue modulates a low-pass biquad filter, opening or dampening the high-frequency content.
  7. Texture & Edge Complexity Detection (Dual Harmony)
    • Local variance (brightness delta between neighboring pixels) calculates spatial texture. Where visual complexity peaks (e.g., cloud formations, coastline boundaries, wildfire plumes), a secondary harmonic voice triggers two scale steps above (a musical third), adding lush polyphony.
  8. Spatialization, Tempo & Ambience
    • Stereo Panning: The horizontal position of the scanline (column 1 to 48) pans the sound dynamically across the stereo field from left to right.
    • Temporal Flow: Each column triggers on an eighth-note (half-beat) division governed by the theme's BPM.
    • Ambient Layer: A generative drone chord and delay/reverb tail accompany the composition, shifting dynamically with overall image luminance.

Algorithmic flow: how Earth Jukebox reads the screen

  1. Capability Detection & Voice Selection (Web Speech API)
    • The narration engine is built on the browser's native Web Speech API (speechSynthesis and SpeechSynthesisUtterance), so it needs no external library or server. At startup a state object (vox) checks whether both interfaces exist in the window; if the browser does not support them, the narration control is hidden and the site simply works without it.
    • The voice is chosen from the list returned by getVoices(): first an en-US voice, then any English voice. Because browsers load voices asynchronously, the selection runs again on the voiceschanged event.
    • The narration is on by default, and the user's choice (on/off) is saved in localStorage, inside a try/catch block so the site keeps working even where storage is blocked.
  2. Speech Engine (Interruption & Sentence Chunking)
    • A single function, speak(text, force), is the only entry point for speech. It ignores empty text, ignores calls when narration is off (unless force is set) and always calls speechSynthesis.cancel() first, so the new message interrupts the previous one and speech never piles up in a queue.
    • The text is split into sentences with a regular expression (cutting at ".", "!" and "?") and each sentence is queued as its own utterance, with language en-US and the selected voice. This gives natural pauses and avoids the cut-offs some browsers cause on long utterances, such as the image descriptions.
  3. Target Discovery &Text Resolution (What Gets Read)
    • Any element matching the selector a, button, summary, label, [data-voz] is a narration target; the closest() method finds the target even when the pointer or focus lands on a child element (an icon inside a button, for example).
    • Text Priority: The spoken text comes from the data-voz attribute first, then the aria-label, and finally the element's own visible text with whitespace normalized. Any element can be made to speak just by receiving data-voz="text".
    • Context-Rich Labels: Where the visible text is not enough, data-voz carries a fuller phrase: the cards say "[name]. Open image and listen.", the piano roll explains that each bar is a note and that clicking jumps to a point in the music, and the speed buttons say "Speed 0.6 times".
    • Always-On Items: The data-voz-always attribute makes an element speak even when narration is off. It is used by the narration button itself, so the user can always hear how to turn it back on.
  4. Triggers: Mouse Hover, Keyboard Focus & Browser Unlock
    • Mouse Hover: A single mouseover listener on the document resolves the target. It ignores the element already announced (vox.last) and waits 150 ms before speaking, cancelling the timer if the pointer moves on, so sweeping the mouse across the page does not produce a burst of speech.
    • Keyboard Focus: A focusin listener speaks immediately when Tab lands on a target, but only if the element matches :focus-visible. Mouse clicks on buttons therefore do not repeat what hover has just announced, and browsers without :focus-visible support fall back to speaking on every focus.
    •  Browser Unlock: Some browsers only allow speech after a user gesture. On the first pointerdown or keydown (captured at the document level) the site speaks a silent, zero-volume utterance to unlock the engine, so the first real message is not lost.
  5. Narration Toggle & Persistent State
    • The narration button (id "voz") exposes its state both visually and to assistive technology: aria-pressed switches between true and false, the label changes between "Narration: on" and "Narration: off", and its data-voz is rewritten to say what a click will do.
    • On click the state is inverted, saved to localStorage and confirmed aloud with "Narration on." or "Narration off." using force, so the user hears the confirmation even when turning narration off. The button has a 44 px minimum height on touch screens.
